text.p: Precious metals markets edged lower in Europe on Monday following an unspectacular end to last week in New York.
They drifted down in the afternoon as New York opened lower in quiet dealings. Dealers said there were few if any incentives for speculators to buy gold at present.
"If the price does not have the aspiration to go up, there is no incentive for a speculator to buy gold," one dealer said.
Gold was fixed at $353.10 per ounce in the afternoon down from $354.20 in the morning and 355.75 on Friday afternoon when the market was at the top of a brief short-covering rally.
At the fixing the Comex February contract was down $1.90 at $354.50 with business limited by some U.S. institutions closing for Martin Luther King Day.
"The emphasis was on the downside earlier when it looked a bit unsure over $354.00. Now it's tried the highs and the lows and is just looking for the range," a dealer said.
Light selling came into Hong Kong which some dealers attributed to Australian producer activity while others maintained the selling was from weak professional longs.
Either way it capped any nascent move firmer.
"There was a bit of light selling (in Europe) this morning which took it below $355.00," one dealer said, while another noted gold was still a $352-$355 market.
Concerns about central bank selling continued to dominate the market outlook following the announcement last Monday that the Dutch central bank had sold 300 tonnes of gold.
"The market is typified by nervousness," one dealer said.
He added that any moves higher in the past week had been related to profit taking on short sales rather than any fresh speculative buying.
Dealers said gold was meeting selling at just over $355.00 with producer selling expected to come in if it approached $356.00.
On the downside support should be secure at $352.00 and $350.00 unless selling intensified.
The other precious metals were quiet around Friday's levels having been largely ignored before Europe opened.
Silver was four cents easier at $4.72/$4.74 but continued to give the impression of having more upside potential than gold. "It has held fairly well compared to gold," a dealer said.
Platinum and palladium were easier but took some support from the continuing silence from Moscow on contract talks for exporting to Japan this year.
"There has been no sign of change there," one dealer said.
Platinum was at $359.00/$360.00 down $1.30 but palladium was barely changed at $120.75/$121.75.
